blurb: "Miss Willmott's ghost" — a green rosette its first year, then a 3–4 ft candelabra of thimble-shaped cones each ringed by a wide, stiff collar of ghost-silver bracts. It blooms, seeds and dies, but it seeds itself so freely that the ghost keeps reappearing somewhere new.
size: ~2–4 ft tall × 1–3 ft wide in its flowering year
water: Low to moderate; medium moisture but drought-tolerant once rooted
spread: Non-running — a single taprooted rosette that dies after flowering, but self-sows freely and perpetuates itself as drifting volunteers
seasons: An evergreen basal rosette overwintering through year one; silvery-blue bracted flower cones June–August in year two; bleached seedhead skeletons standing into winter before the plant dies
wildlife: Bumblebees and honeybees work the cones heavily; a strong midsummer nectar plant
toxic: No significant toxicity reported to people or pets; the bracts are stiff and sharply spined
habitat: Subalpine meadows and open rocky mountain slopes

care.hardiness: Rated USDA zones 4–7, so cold is no problem in Boulder's 5b–6a; the overwintering rosette is fully hardy here.[1] Zone 7 as an upper limit is a heat/humidity ceiling, not something the Front Range runs into.
care.planting: This is a biennial: plant or sow it in spring after the mid-May last frost (or in fall)[4] and expect a rosette the first year and flowers the second.[1] It is taprooted, transplants poorly and is best left undisturbed, so put it where you want it the first time.[1] It grows more compactly in containers, which is a genuinely good option for a plant this architectural — use a deep pot with free-draining mix and let it overwinter outside.[1]
care.sun: Full sun.[1] In less than full sun the flowering stems sprawl and the silver bract colour washes out.[1]
care.soil: Medium-moisture, well-drained soil; unusually for a sea holly it prefers moist, fertile ground rather than starvation rations.[1] That said, tall plants still sprawl in overly fertile soils, so 'decent garden soil with real drainage' is the target — not a heavily manured bed, and not baked clay.[1]
care.water: Medium moisture needs with good drought tolerance once established.[1] Of the sea hollies in this guide it is the least xeric — give it an occasional deep summer soak in a dry Front Range July rather than treating it as no-water.
care.spacing: Space 18–24 in apart to suit its 1–3 ft spread.[1] Taller plants may need support, particularly in rich soil or wind — a discreet ring or a neighbouring shrub to lean on is easier than staking each stem.[1]
care.propagation: Easily grown from seed, which is the only sensible route: it is monocarpic, so the parent dies after flowering and there is no clump left to divide.[1] Let a few heads shed where you want next year's plants, or collect seed and sow it fresh.
care.sow: Sow fresh seed in fall, outdoors or in deep pots left outside, so it gets natural winter chilling; seedlings resent root disturbance, so thin rather than transplant, and move volunteers only while they are tiny.
care.bloom: Flowers June to August in bluish-silver cones, each held in a wide ruff of stiff, spiny, silver-white bracts that are the real show.[1] Superb as a fresh cut flower and it dries beautifully — the bracts hold their ghost-silver colour.
care.feeding: None needed; extra fertility mainly buys you sprawling stems.[1] If the soil is very poor, a spring topdressing of compost is enough.
care.maintenance: Low. The single decision that matters is deadheading: these eryngiums self-seed and remain in the garden year after year as if they were perennial unless the spent flower heads are removed before seed drop.[1] Since the plant dies after seeding, deadheading everything means no plant next year — leave several heads to shed, cut the rest. Leave the skeletons standing for winter structure and clear them in early spring.[3]
care.selfsow: Freely — this is the whole survival strategy of a monocarpic plant, and the reason a 'ghost' turns up in a different corner of the border each year.[1] Move volunteers while they are seedlings (the taproot forms fast), and deadhead hard if you want to confine it.
care.troubles: No serious insect or disease problems, though taller plants may need support.[1] The genus is susceptible to leaf and bud eelworms, slugs and snails, root rot and powdery mildews.[3] Do not read the plant's death after flowering as a failure — it is monocarpic and that is the normal life cycle.[1]

edible.summary: An ornamental and a dried-flower plant — Eryngium giganteum has no documented food use and is not considered dangerously poisonous.[1]
edible.caution: No authority documents this species as edible; treat it as inedible. The genus does contain real foods — candied 'eryngo' roots came from Eryngium maritimum and E. campestre, and culantro (E. foetidum) is a culinary herb — but edibility in the carrot family is species-by-species and cannot be generalised from a relative; the same family contains poison hemlock. The everyday hazard here is mechanical: the bracts are stiff and genuinely sharp, so cut and handle it with gloves.[3]
